summary: Round 2, test-reviewer lane (testability the rows prescribe; no code, no tests in this diff). All three round-1 majors are addressed with prescriptions that a bare-pair dedup, a skip-and-return refusal, and a format-only M4.10c would each now fail. All six baked-in line references resolve in the current tree and each carries enough quoted prose to survive drift, so M4.26's objection to line offsets lands only weakly here. Three minors remain, each with a named mutation that a future implementer's tests would still not have to kill.

A dedup on the bare (podId, flushSeq) refuses that commit, so the prescribed test fails against it. The three previously unnamed mutations (< for <=, single fleet-wide long, in-process-only) are now named at :269-274, with the CheckpointWriterContentTest:118-128 strictly-lower habit cited as the reason <= must be pinned.

findings.title: M4.10d pins WHICH key the retry gets back but never pins the OFFSETS, so a no-op dedup survives every stated criterion
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: make the dedup a no-op -- record lastAppliedFlushSeq per pod, checkpoint it, recover it across a takeover, and NEVER consult it on the commit path. Walk every clause the row states. (a) 'refuse a replayed (podId, flushSeq)': the row's only stated observable of the refusal is that the retrying caller gets the ORIGINAL segment key back. Under the no-op the retry is committed afresh and the returned delta carries the SUBMITTED segment key, which is the same key -- so a test asserting delta.segments() contains request.segmentKey() is GREEN, the append completes normally, and the skip-and-return prohibition at :260-267 is satisfied. (b) 'a restarted pod reissuing 0 for a NEW segment must be ACCEPTED': green, the no-op accepts everything. (c) 'a single fleet-wide long for the per-pod map': green, the map is per-pod and populated. (d) 'a dedup that only works in-process': green, the window is recovered because M4.10c carried it. The ONLY thing the no-op breaks is the parent row's stated harm -- the retried pod is assigned offsets TWICE -- and no clause in M4.10d requires the retry to receive the SAME firstOffset as the first attempt, nor that the chain gain no second entry. This is conspicuous because the row names five other mutations explicitly; the one assertion that actually kills the no-op is the unnamed one, and the concrete guidance the row does give ('the ORIGINAL segment key is returned') points at the assertion that does NOT kill it. The tree has this exact failure on record: M4.27 documents an M4.20 row whose criteria were left unpinned and which a first test reviewer passed. SUGGESTED (one sentence, no round three needed -- commit body or a follow-up row): the retry must receive the FIRST attempt's assigned firstOffset for its runs, and the chain must not gain a second entry for the replayed pair; assert both, not just the key.

findings.title: The end-to-end anchor M4.10c owns is satisfied by checkpoint-only recovery, so it does not exercise the delta change it exists to justify
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: leave CommitDelta UNCHANGED and recover the pod window on takeover by reading the last CHECKPOINT instead. Walk the prescribed anchor: CheckpointWriterContentTest.theFirstCheckpointAfterATakeoverCarriesNoPodsAtAll builds the first writer with everyDeltas = 1 (CheckpointWriter.java:87), so poda's 42 is already inside a WRITTEN checkpoint before the successor CommitLog recovers. Seeding pods from that checkpoint makes the inverted assertion (successor's first checkpoint carries poda -> 42) GREEN with no format change at all, and the mutation is invisible. The gap it leaves in production is the commits made AFTER the last checkpoint and before the takeover -- exactly the window M4.10c says the delta must carry -- and the fixture as prescribed cannot contain one. This does not make the row wrong (M4.10b may legitimately conclude checkpoint recovery suffices and void M4.10c), but it means the anchor cannot distinguish the design M4.10c exists to pay for. SUGGESTED: state that the fixture must commit at least once AFTER the last checkpoint and before the takeover -- e.g. everyDeltas = 2 with a single commit of poda 42 -- so that a checkpoint-only recovery fails and only a delta-carried window passes.

findings.title: The golden ORDER lesson names the hazard but not the tier, and the nearest test to hand is measured NOT to detect it
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: delete the encoder's sort for the new keyed field. An implementer reading 'If the new field is a keyed collection, pin its ORDER too -- delete-the-sort survives a read-from-disk golden' most naturally adds an order assertion beside the existing one in GoldenCheckpointTest.theGoldenBytesCarryStreamsAndPodsInASCENDINGOrder -- and that class's own javadoc (GoldenCheckpointTest.java:25-29) records the MEASURED result that 'both delete-the-sort mutations leave all three tests here GREEN, because nothing in this class builds a fixture -- it reads committed bytes', naming CheckpointTest's order tests as the ones that actually constrain the encoder. So the row's warning, followed literally, lands the assertion in the one file that cannot kill the mutation it warns about; what a read-from-disk golden DOES pin (per :31-35) is the record's order-preserving copy, a different mutation. SUGGESTED: name the tier -- pin the new field's order in a fixture-BUILDING encode test alongside CheckpointTest's order tests, not only in the golden.

not_findings_but_worth_the_commit_body: backlog-notes.md:253-256 says 'A cross-leader-change fixture has one incarnation of poda, so whatever M4.10b makes durable never varies.' That holds for a POD-scoped token (a start-time nonce, or SegmentKey's timestamp+per-pod sequence) but not for the LEASE epoch, which is leader-scoped and varies across exactly that fixture. The prescription is unaffected -- the pod-restart test is the right discriminator either way, and under a leader-scoped epoch it is the test that exposes the epoch as insufficient (the restarted pod keeps the same epoch, so an epoch-qualified key still refuses its legitimate flushSeq 0). Only the justifying clause over-generalises. Worth noting because it also means the cross-takeover case is NOT redundant under a leader-scoped key: there it shows an epoch-qualified key wrongly ACCEPTING a replay across a term. The row keeps that case anyway via the in-process-only mutation at :272-274.
